summary: The text asks how to estimate the transmission rate $\beta$ of an SIR model from noisy case counts. It proposes a physics-informed neural network that learns the epidemic trajectory and $\beta$ jointly, and reports accurate recovery of a constant $\beta$ but instability for time-varying $\beta(t)$ and an identifiability problem with unknown reporting rates.
key_points: Estimating $\beta$ and $\gamma$ from case counts is an inverse problem that can be ill-posed.
The PINN loss combines data misfit, ODE residual at collocation points and initial-condition penalties.
A constant $\beta$ was recovered within 5% from 20 noisy observations in a synthetic experiment.
A time-varying $\beta(t)$ required a smoothness penalty to be stable.
With an unknown reporting fraction $\rho$, $\rho$ and the initial infected are not jointly identifiable early in an epidemic.
methods: Neural network $u_\theta(t)$ approximating $(S, I, R)$ with $\beta$ as a trainable parameter
results: Time-varying $\beta(t)$ unstable without a smoothness penalty
limitations: Residual enforced only at collocation points
Results sensitive to the loss weights $\lambda_r, \lambda_0$
Only synthetic data; no comparison with classical least-squares fitting (reader's note)
open_questions: Can the method be extended to metapopulation models on contact networks with node-wise transmission rates?
How should the loss weights be chosen in a principled way?
